## Lessons extraction — 9 commits

**a5ab95f** — `main()` named `parseBlockedBy` without importing it; the line lived inside a loop that had been empty in every run for 3 days, so nothing threw despite a fully green suite.
Lesson: a code path reachable only through untested I/O against a live Action (e.g. `main`) can carry a plain `ReferenceError` indefinitely if the branch that hits it happens to be empty every run. Extract such logic into an exported pure function a test can call directly, rather than trusting "green suite" as evidence the line ever executed.

**8e9a4f3** — merge commit, no content. Nothing.

**ad122c6** — retiring two migration tolerances (cron format, legacy frequency spellings) once fleet-wide gates were met. This just executes the already-documented pattern (gate tolerance removal on a converge-confirmable precondition, empty-not-delete the map). Nothing new.

**c7354ec** — the update task's precondition used to *guess* whether a member was behind canon via a proxy ("local mount converged, no pack moved locally"), which answers a different question than "is canon ahead of me" and silently starved two members of updates for days with no self-healing path.
Lesson: when a precondition cannot observe the actual condition it's meant to gate (canon's state, here, is structurally unavailable to a scheduler run), don't substitute a proxy that measures something else — pick the cheaper failure mode explicitly (always run, accept occasional no-ops) rather than decline-by-default, when declining wrongly is unrecoverable and running wrongly is just a wasted converge.

**90dab0c** — the drain gate re-read the queue from GitHub to decide whether to dispatch an executor; that list read is eventually consistent and missed issues created 377–584ms earlier, so a forced wake's own freshly-created ready item was invisible and got stuck until the next cron.
Lesson: don't confirm your own just-written effect via a re-read from an eventually-consistent API — union the read with what this run itself is known to have written.

**2d25d2b** — dropped an explanatory comment (about why a workflow doesn't serialize the whole secrets context) from a vendored workflow stub, moving the reason to where the decision is implemented; also taught the `consumer-safe-change` check to strip YAML comments so a comment-only stub edit doesn't false-positive as a "contract surface" needing a migration record.
Lesson: for a file vendored byte-for-byte to every member forever and never read by anything (a workflow stub), comments are pure freight — the rationale belongs beside the code that implements the decision, not on the copy. A contract-change detector comparing such files should diff on structure, not text, or trivial comment churn triggers false migration-record demands.

**379cc01** (paired with **fd4cb68**, which introduced the reverted shape — no separate new lesson) — `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}` is exactly the shape GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags; a flagged workflow silently parks with zero jobs pending human "Approve," which an unattended queue reads as indistinguishable from "nothing pickable." It had been eating executor runs fleet-wide for ~2 days before catch.
Lesson: never pass GitHub Actions' whole `secrets` context via `toJSON(secrets)` — it triggers platform malicious-workflow detection and silently blocks unattended runs behind a human click, with no error signal the automation can see.

**723b272** — the fleet dashboard used to read each member end-to-end before starting the next; when the viewer's rate-limit budget ran out mid-sweep, the *last* members in the roster were entirely unread (misread as "nothing on fire") while the first members got full decoration.
Lesson: when a bounded, exhaustible budget (rate limit) covers a batch sweep over many independent items, order work horizontally — one cheap, high-value pass across every item before any item gets the next, deeper pass — so a budget shortfall degrades every row equally (missing decoration) instead of erasing the tail of the list entirely.

All four PRs are solo-authored and self-merged by the same author (missingbulb) with zero review comments/threads on every one — so the review-discussion channel is empty across the board; what follows is drawn from PR bodies + diffs.

**PR #1357: nothing new, but confirms the pattern from #1355** — the missing `parseBlockedBy` import sat in `main()`'s dead code for 3 days because the loop it lived in never ran. The fix (extracting `blockersToResolve()` as an exported, directly-testable function) is really the same lesson #1355 already teaches below, applied a second time to the same file. Not counting separately.

**PR #1355: lesson.** What happened: `listMarkedIssues` queried GitHub's issues API with `labels=markA,markB` under a comment claiming "the label filter is OR across a comma-separated list" — it's actually AND (conjunctive), so the query silently matched zero issues for 3+ days across 40+ green scheduler runs, while a failed read (`status !== 200`) was also collapsed into the same "empty list" branch as a genuinely-empty one.

Candidate lesson: *GitHub's `issues?labels=a,b` query parameter is a conjunctive AND across the comma-separated list, not an OR — a wrong assumption here silently zeroes out results rather than erroring. When querying by multiple independent labels, issue one listing per label and union the results; and never let a failed API read (non-200) collapse into the same code path as a legitimately-empty result — throw instead, or a broken lane looks identical to "nothing to do" indefinitely.* Grounded in the PR body: "under a comment asserting `The label filter is OR across a comma-separated list`. It is conjunctive" and "A failed read was an empty read... Both listings now throw instead."

**PR #1352: lesson.** What happened: a prior PR (#1329) tried to delete both `engine/scheduler/` and `updates/` shim trees together; this PR explains why that was wrong and splits them. The `updates/` tree looked deletable by local static-import search ("nothing in the canon imports it... only tests reference it") but is actually resolved at runtime via a fresh clone of canon HEAD (`git clone --depth 1 CANON_URL`, then dynamic `import()`), from paths named inside **already-vendored** member workers — code living in other repos' checked-out copies, invisible to any grep of this repo.

Candidate lesson: *Before deleting a directory, verify what resolves against it isn't limited to this repo's own static imports — check for dynamic/runtime resolution (a fresh clone + `import()` by path, a template stamped into other repos) that a local grep can't see. #1329 deleted `updates/` and "without repointing those calls, despite its body claiming otherwise," which "fails every member's next update at module resolution, unrepairable, because the repair *is* the update."* This is non-obvious specifically because the two shim trees looked structurally identical (both "legacy paths kept for compat") but had different retirement gates for exactly this reason.

**PR #1350: nothing new.** The PR carefully gates two migration-tolerance retirements on fleet-wide readiness verified by reading actual member state (all 13 workflows, a sweep of local pack declarations) rather than a calendar date, and empties (not deletes) `LEGACY_FREQUENCIES` so it can be refilled later. Both practices are already codified verbatim in the repo's existing local rules (`Scheduling the removal of a temporary compatibility tolerance — gate it on a converge-cycle-confirmable precondition`, `Changing an export in updates/* — empty it, never remove it`), so this is routine, well-executed application of settled convention rather than a new lesson.

**Summary of candidates to land:** two lessons, both from the `parseBlockedBy`/`listMarkedIssues` incident (#1355, reinforced by #1357) and one from the shim-deletion split (#1352).

{"number":1160,"title":"Verify in production: an extension repo still ships to the store now the pipeline never bumps","body":"#1151 took the version write out of the `chrome-extension` release pipeline. The daily
auto-release used to patch-bump the manifest + `package.json` and push that to `main` before
packaging; it now writes nothing and instead asks whether the version already on `main` has a
release yet. The bump moved into the change that earns it (`cer/version-bumped`), and a
deliberate minor/major is a `mode: bump` dispatch calling a new vendored reusable
(`chrome-extension-bump-version.yml`).

**Why this could not be watched at merge time.** The checks are unit-tested and the vendoring
round-trip is covered, but nothing in this repo executes a GitHub Actions workflow. The changed
behaviour — "is a release due?" — only runs in a member repo, on its own schedule, after the
nightly converge materialises the new stubs. Its failure mode is silent in the direction that
matters: a wrong condition means the extension quietly stops reaching the Chrome Web Store,
with a green-looking no-op run.

Original-issue: #1150
In-production-when: `missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`'s `.claudinite-checks.json` stamps `packVersions['chrome-extension']` at `60821.1` or higher, AND `.github/workflows/chrome-extension-bump-version.yml` exists on its default branch.
Verify: on that repo — (a) `.github/workflows/chrome-extension-daily-release.yml` carries a step named "Has the version on main been released yet?" and declares no `bump:` job; (b) the most recent "Release to Chrome Store" run that started after the converge concluded `success`; (c) no open issue labelled `workflow-failure` whose title names "Release: Daily Auto-Release" was created after the converge. PASS = all three. A run that shipped and one that reported the version already released are both passes — the assertion is that the pipeline reached a terminal state without failing, not that it released.
Not-before: 2026-08-24T02:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

Model: sonnet

The reference implementation is named here because canon holds no repo list by design; if that
repo has not converged but another extension repo has, read that one instead and say which.

## For the run

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact — that repo's committed
   `.claudinite-checks.json` and its `.github/workflows/` tree. Never infer it from this repo's
   merge, a green CI run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the stamped pack
   version, the workflow run URL and its conclusion) and close this issue as completed. Fails:
   reopen #1150 with a comment saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you
   read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed — finding the fault is
   this verification doing its job.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, clear this issue's
   `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

{"number":1240,"title":"Remove the tidy-branches task from tidy-repo","body":"Drop `tidy-branches` from the `tidy-repo` pack. The pack keeps its other two dimensions, `tidy-issues` and `tidy-prs`; only the branch sweep goes.

## The change

Delete `packs/tidy-repo/tasks/tidy-branches/` (both `task.mjs` and `task.md`) and sweep every reference to it. Known referencing files:

- `packs/tidy-repo/pack.mjs` — the task roster
- `packs/tidy-repo/pack.test.mjs` — assertions naming the task
- `packs/tidy-repo/README.md`
- `packs/tidy-repo/RULES.md` — names the three tasks and the "branches — assess only" half of the policy
- `packs/tidy-repo/tasks/tidy-issues/task.md` — mentions it
- `packs/tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md` — its worker skill

Decide as part of the work whether `single-branch-status` goes with it: with no task invoking it, it is a skill nothing calls. Removing it is the default; keep it only if something outside `tidy-branches` still reaches it, and say which in the PR.

`RULES.md` currently states the policy over three dimensions and specifically covers branches ("assess only; never delete, push, merge, or close"). With the task gone, that prose has no runner — rewrite the policy to the two dimensions that remain rather than leaving branch rules stranded.

Do not edit `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`; it is generated and holds historical counts.

## Done looks like

- No `tidy-branches` anywhere outside generated files and historical records (`git grep tidy-branches` clean).
- `packs/tidy-repo` pack version bumped (the `pack-version-bumped` check requires it for any pack change).
- Full suite green: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`.
- The task's standing tracker issue, if one is open in this repo, gets a closing comment saying the task was removed — the sweep will never rewrite it again.

{"number":1188,"title":"Nothing prunes an absorbed pack's leftover directory from a member's mount","body":"Blocked-by: #1187

Model: opus

When a pack is **absorbed** into another (`chrome-extension-release` → `chrome-extension`, `github-actions` → `git-github`, `firebase-release` → `firebase` — #1057, #1079), its directory stays in every member's mount forever. The pack flow "replaces a declared pack's tree wholesale but never removes a tree that has stopped being declared" (`engine/migrations/2026-08-19-pack-renames/migration.mjs`), and no migration record covers the absorptions — grep finds none.

After #1187 those leftovers are inert rather than fatal, so this is dead weight, not breakage: a complete, loadable copy of a retired pack sitting beside its survivor in seven members' trees.

**Why a rename record doesn't fit.** The rename records work by `aliases`, which *move* the legacy directory onto the canonical path, and depend on "the canonical side does not exist yet" — for an absorption the survivor's directory is already there, so the move cannot apply. The action here is a **delete**, which the record vocabulary has no shape for today.

**Done looks like**: a member's converge removes `.claudinite/shared/packs//` for each absorbed pack, and a member that already converged past the record still gets there. Confirm against a real member tree, not only a fixture — the same way #1186 was confirmed.

**Ruled out**: doing it inside #1187. That change unfreezes the fleet and stays scoped to the loader; a destructive sweep over members' trees is a separate concern with its own risk.

Worth checking while here whether the absorbed ids can start coming out of `RENAMED_PACKS` — its own retirement rule is "no member's declaration and no member's stamped `packVersions` still carries that spelling", which several members still do.

{"number":1166,"title":"Retire the fleet-usage task and usage-fleet.GENERATED.json","body":"The destructive tail of #1158. The fleet-wide usage aggregate has no reader left: it was a stateless recompute over the members' own files, it held no longer history than they do (their week rows are append-once and never pruned), and the fleet dashboard now reads each member's file directly — as the viewer, which is also the permission-correct source. Its `coverage` census is derived live: a rostered member with no usage file *is* the absent row.

The last thing it was needed for was being the fleet page's **roster**, which #1165 replaces with live enumeration of a configured `owner`.

## The change

In this repo (the canon):

- delete `packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-usage/` — the task, `worker.mjs`, `aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs`, their tests and the task README;
- remove its row from the `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` pack README's task catalog;
- bump the sheepdog pack's version, with the reason in the version comment;
- check `.gitattributes` for a `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json merge=ours` entry and drop it if this repo carries one;
- grep the corpus for `usage-fleet` and `fleet-usage` and clean up what is left — `docs/skill-usage-metrics/DESIGN.md` §6 already carries a superseded note, so update it to past tense rather than adding a second one.

In Shepherd (a separate change, by whoever holds that repo): delete `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` and its `.gitattributes` entry. The file is harmless while it sits there, so this is tidiness rather than a blocker.

## Done looks like

The canon carries no `fleet-usage` task and no code that reads or writes a fleet-wide usage aggregate; the sheepdog pack's README and version reflect that; the full suite and `check_the_world` are green; and Shepherd's fleet dashboard still renders (it reads members' files, not this one).

## Do not start before

Both preconditions below are real, not formalities. The task must not be deleted while anything still reads its output.

1. **#1165 is merged** — that is what stops the fleet page reading `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` as its roster.
2. **Shepherd's `claudinite-dashboard` declaration has been flipped** from `"rosterFile": "usage-fleet.GENERATED.json"` to `"owner": "missingbulb"`. Until that lands, Shepherd's deployed page is still resolving its member list from this file, and deleting the task would freeze that list at whatever it last held. Verify it at Shepherd's HEAD before touching anything here.

If the second is not true yet, close nothing and change nothing: comment saying which precondition is outstanding and leave this issue for the next pick.

## Summary

All four PRs are solo Claude Code sessions merged by the same author with **zero review comments/threads** — no back-and-forth to mine. Lessons below come from the diff + PR body reasoning only.

**PR #1342 — drain gate missed work items it just created**
What happened: the scheduler's "is anything pickable" gate re-read the issue list from GitHub right after creating/readying items, and on 3 members the just-written issue wasn't in that read yet — the run reported an empty queue and skipped dispatch, leaving a **forced** wake stuck `task:ready` until the next cron (no way to override, since the precondition re-runs at pick).

Lesson: **GitHub's issue-list API is eventually consistent — a read immediately after your own write can miss what you just created (measured gap: 377–584ms).** Any gate that reads back state it just wrote should union its own record of what it wrote with the read, rather than trusting the read alone. Non-obvious because "successful, green run silently drops its own work" — nothing goes red, the tracker just reads as converged. Fix: `pickableCount(open, readiedThisRun)` unions `listOpenWorkItems()` with a `Set` of issue numbers the run itself readied this invocation.

**PR #1337 — GitHub flags `toJSON(secrets)` in a workflow as malicious**
What happened: #1301 had collapsed all repo secrets into one line, `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}`, specifically to avoid making the executor workflow a function of the task set (a prior wedge, #1296). That shape turned out to be exactly what GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags — the run parks with **zero jobs** pending a human Approve click, which from the queue's side is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable." It silently ate executor runs fleet-wide for hours before being caught.

Lesson: **never serialize the whole `secrets` context (`toJSON(secrets)`) into an unattended GitHub Actions workflow — GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags it and parks the run behind manual approval with zero jobs, which is silent and looks like an empty queue rather than a failure.** Name secrets individually even though it costs a human-merged PR per new secret (`.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge can't write) — the PR body states the owner explicitly chose "a rare human-merged PR beats a permanent human click on every run." Grounded in the reverted line itself and the stub guard test added: `assert.ok(!/toJSON\(\s*secrets\s*\)/.test(...))`.

**PR #1348 — precondition guessed at unavailable information, guessed wrong, stalled silently**
What happened: an update-task precondition declined to run when "the mount converged and no pack moved locally," treating that as a proxy for "member is current." But the scheduler Action deliberately never reads canon (DESIGN §3.3), so that signal is equally true of a current member and one canon moved past an hour after its own converge — it stalled two members 4 packs behind for a day, immune even to a forced wake (the precondition re-evaluates at pick).

Lesson: **when a precondition cannot observe the actual signal it needs to answer its question, don't let it guess via a correlated-but-different proxy — weigh the asymmetry explicitly.** Here declining wrongly caused permanent, silent staleness nothing in the member could repair, while running wrongly cost one no-op converge/day; the PR removed the guess entirely rather than tune the proxy. Grounded in the PR body: "declining wrongly costs permanent, silent staleness that nothing in the member can repair; running wrongly costs one converge that finds nothing and exits."

**PR #1338: nothing.** A `consumer-safe-change` check fired on a comment-only stub diff and the fix (strip comments before diffing head/base) is a straightforward instance of already-existing canon rules (comment-stripping for checks; "if a comment narrates a past fix, keep only what's still true") — not a new lesson.

{"number":1235,"title":"Chain 1/3: force the twice-daily cron onto every member, and read it back","body":"Link 1 of #1225's execution chain. You will never see the conversation that planned this — everything you need is here.

```
Blocked-by: #1231
Model: sonnet
```

## What changed, and why this needs forcing

The scheduler cron went from hourly to twice daily (`docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §17): ` ,<(dailyHour+12)%24> * * *`. That is a change to a contract members' own files must satisfy — a workflow file plus a frequency vocabulary — so the nightly converge is not enough on its own to answer *"did it work on every repo?"*.

## What makes this step's world ready

#1231 closed, meaning #1230 merged. The queue holds this until then.

## The playbook

1. Drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, so it converges every member and reports per member rather than dispatching and returning.
2. For **each** member, read two things from the member's own repo:
   - its stamp's `packVersions` — `claudinite-lifecycle` ≥ `60822.2`, `claudinite-growth` ≥ `60822.1`, `claudinite-dashboard` ≥ `60822.2`;
   - its `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` `cron:` line.
3. The cron is member-specific. Compute the expected value rather than matching a constant: `node engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs ` for the minute, and the member's own `taskScheduler.dailyHour` (default 4) for the hours — so a default member expects ` 4,16 * * *`.

## What counts as this step having worked

Every member reads back **both** the stamped pack versions and its own correct two-tick cron.

The workflow file is the half that can lag: `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push, so it lands through the member's `update` task apply-stage PR. A member whose stamp has moved but whose workflow PR is still open has **not** passed — note it and keep this issue open; it will pass on a later run once that PR lands.

## When the check fails

Comment what you actually read, per member, and **leave this issue open**. Closing is what releases the next link, so a failed step must not close.

A member you cannot read is a failure, not a pass. A scope-blocked or rate-limited sweep answers "all clear" in exactly the way a healthy fleet does — if a read did not succeed, say so rather than counting it.

## How it ends

Comment the per-member evidence on #1225, then close this issue as completed. That close releases Link 2.

But `queue/instructions.md` step 6 *is* session-side — it is the procedure every agent session follows to converge the one work item it was fired for (a Claude Code session, not an Actions job). {"number":1346,"title":"Move taskScheduler from a top-level settings key into the claudinite-tasks pack's own config","body":"`.claudinite-settings.json` carries `taskScheduler` as a **top-level key**, beside `packs`, `accept` and `sharedConstants`:

```json
"taskScheduler": {
  "agenticTaskInvocationEndpoints": { "default": { "url": "…", "tokenSecret": "CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN" } },
  "dailyHour": 4,
  "weeklyDay": "Sun",
  "monthlyDay": 1
}
```

Every one of those settings belongs to `claudinite-tasks`. Now that the task surface is a pack (#1317) and every member declares it, this is settings for a pack sitting outside that pack's declaration — where every other pack's settings live in its own `config` block (`barriers` rules, `claude-code-web-users-support` store, `claudinite-dashboard` mode, `node` dirs). A repo that does not declare `claudinite-tasks` can still carry a `taskScheduler` block that nothing reads.

Target shape:

```json
{ "id": "claudinite-tasks", "config": { "dailyHour": 4, "weeklyDay": "Sun", "monthlyDay": 1, "agenticTaskInvocationEndpoints": { … } } }
```

## What it touches

`taskScheduler` is read at **46 sites across 17 modules**. The ones that matter:

- `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs` — `loadConfig`, plus `ENDPOINTS_KEY` / `LEGACY_ENDPOINTS_KEY`; the natural place for a single resolver every other caller goes through.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/` — `converge-workflows.mjs`, `hash-minute.mjs`, `calendar`/anchors, `queue/scheduler-run.mjs`, `queue/executor.mjs`, `queue/invoke.mjs`, `task-contract.mjs`, `signals/fleet.mjs`, `worldRules/task-declaration-shape.mjs`, `tasks/task-janitor/queue-sweep.mjs`.
- `packs/claudinite-dashboard/` — `view-repo.mjs`, `fleet.mjs` (cross-pack readers of the same block).
- `engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs` — retiring with the shims, check whether it still needs touching when this runs.
- `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` — fixtures spell the shape and will need both forms while the tolerance stands.

## Done looks like

- One resolver owns the lookup; no module reaches into either shape directly.
- The reader **accepts the legacy top-level key at the door** and keeps doing so — this is the accept-legacy-input rule, so nothing waits on stragglers. A member on the old shape keeps working indefinitely.
- A migration record moves the block into the pack entry for every member that declares `claudinite-tasks`, preserving the values exactly (`dailyHour` in particular, since the hashed cron is derived from it and a changed value silently reschedules the repo).
- The tolerance's removal is gated on **no member still stamping the top-level key**, read off the stamps — never a date. That is a separate change, not this one.
- `.claudinite-settings.json`'s schema (whatever `$schema` points at) reflects the new shape.

## Watch for

- **`dailyHour` is load-bearing.** `hashedCron` takes the repo's full name *and* `dailyHour`; if the migration drops or defaults it, the repo's cron minute and anchor hours move and its queue quietly reschedules. Assert the regenerated cron is byte-identical before and after on a real member's settings.
- **The endpoint token name is a secret name, not a secret.** It rides into the executor workflow's env via `declaredSecrets`; moving the block must not change the generated secret list, or every member needs a workflow PR.
- **`claudinite-dashboard` reads it cross-pack.** It has no dependency on `claudinite-tasks` and must not gain one — the resolver's home needs to be somewhere both can reach, which is the engine helper, not the pack.

**PR #1335 — Ship the tasks pack in the engine lane while the legacy shims name it**

What happened: A shim in `engine/scheduler/` re-exports a file that lives in `packs/claudinite-tasks/`. Because the engine and pack lanes deliver to members on separate update cycles, a member could receive the new engine (with the shim) before receiving the pack version the shim points at — the shim resolves to nothing, the pack fails to load, and the self-test gate refuses to land the converge. That also blocks the member from receiving the very pack update that would fix it. Nothing in the test suite caught it; only a live canary run did.

Candidate lesson: **A re-export shim is not sufficient on its own — its target must ship in the *same lane* as the shim for as long as the shim exists**, because "the fielded-import scan asks whether a path resolves in the canon, which it did, and the rehearsal fixtures are all built from the current canon, so none of them holds the older pack version that makes the window visible." Existing canon prose already says "leave a shim" when retiring a cross-lane import; this PR shows that rule is incomplete when the shim's *target* is itself a file that migrates lanes — the target has to travel with it, not just the pointer.

**PR #1302 — Pass the whole secrets context to the executor in one static line**

What happened: routine, well-reasoned refactor (switched from enumerating secrets by name in the workflow to `${{ toJSON(secrets) }}`), no friction visible in the diff or discussion.

Candidate lesson: the author flagged an unverified GitHub Actions masking gotcha worth remembering for any future work with `toJSON(secrets)`: "masking is registered per exact literal, so a secret containing `"`, `\` or a newline appears JSON-escaped in the bag and would not be masked if something printed it." Non-obvious because it inverts the usual assumption that GitHub always masks secret values regardless of encoding — here JSON-escaping breaks the literal match masking depends on. (The author also couldn't verify this against `docs.github.com`, blocked by egress proxy — already covered by the standing rule on policy-boundary fetch blocks, so not a new lesson on its own.)

**PR #1315 — Cut the local pack's RULES.md to one trigger and directive per rule**

Nothing new. This PR is the commit that *introduced* the "≈40 words, one trigger, one directive, split rules that carry two situations" header rule already visible verbatim at the top of the current `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`. It's applying the existing `authoring-agent-docs` skill's guidance, not discovering a new one. Its other notable move — deleting a local rule because it contradicted a canon rule loaded in the same session — is exactly what the existing `growth-dedup` skill already governs.

**PR #1314 — Fleet dashboard: read the fleet horizontally, one pass at a time**

What happened: the fleet sweep read each member end-to-end (depth-first) under four-way concurrency; hitting the rate-limit budget mid-sweep meant the *tail* of the roster got nothing while early members got full decoration, silently reading as "nothing on fire." Rewritten to read breadth-first — every member through pass N before any member starts pass N+1.

Candidate lesson: **when a batch/fleet read operates under a budget that can run out mid-sweep, prefer a breadth-first (one pass across the whole set) order over depth-first (each item read to completion before the next starts)**, so a shortfall degrades every row's least-important panel uniformly instead of leaving some fraction of the set completely unread and indistinguishable from healthy. Grounded in: "Read a member end to end before starting the next and the budget is spent depth-first: the first members get their decoration before the last members are looked at at all... A budget that runs out now costs the same panel on every row rather than the last members entirely." This is a generically reusable pattern for any rate-limited fleet/roster sweep, not specific to this dashboard.

{"number":1351,"title":"Verify in production: no member goes red on the tightened cron and frequency checks","body":"#1233's retirement landed as `ad122c6` (#1350). Two tolerances came out, and both feed **blocking** checks that run in every member:

- `scheduler-workflow-shape` no longer accepts an hourly cron line.
- `LEGACY_FREQUENCIES` is empty, so a task declaration naming a retired token fails `validateTaskDeclaration`.

The failure mode is worth catching quickly: a member that slipped through goes **blocking-red on its own CI**, and `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot repair, so it would need a hand-merged PR to clear.

{"number":1353,"title":"Delete the updates/ shims, once no member's vendored worker names them","body":"The second half of L4. #1352 deleted the `engine/scheduler/` shims and repointed the update worker at `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/*`; the `updates/*` re-export tree itself is still there, deliberately.

## Why it could not go with the first half

The worker resolves its flows against a **fresh canon clone at HEAD**, not the member's own mount:

```js
git(['clone', '--depth', '1', CANON_URL, tmp]);
const load = async (rel) => import(pathToFileURL(join(tmp, rel)).href);
```

So the surface a member calls is whatever **its vendored worker** names, resolved against whatever canon looks like at that moment. Every member vendored a worker naming `updates/*` on 2026-08-24. Deleting the tree before they field the repointed worker fails their next update at module resolution — and nothing can repair it, because the repair *is* the update. That is the failure `basics/RULES.md` names: *"Changing an export in `updates/*` — empty it, never remove it."*

## The gate

**No member's vendored worker names `updates/`.** Read it off the members, never off this repo's tree and never off a date:

```
.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs
```

on each member's default branch — every one must call `load('packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/…')`. A member still on the old spelling has not converged past #1352 yet, and deleting the tree strands it.

That gate is met only after every member converges to `claudinite-lifecycle 60824.6` or higher, so the check is worth making after the fleet has had a night.

## What to do when it is met

- Delete `updates/` whole — `engine-update.mjs`, `pack-update.mjs`, `terminals.mjs`, `install.mjs`, `legacy-entry.mjs`, `README.md`.
- Drop the three `updates/*` entries from `install.test.mjs`'s `fielded` map, leaving the `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/*` ones. The comment there explains why both were listed; it comes out with them.

{"number":1347,"title":"Merge the dispatch simulator into the scheduler codebase — the sim becomes a test harness","body":"`packs/claudinite-tasks/test/sim/sim.mjs` (1310 lines) imports **nothing** from the engine: it is a second implementation of the dispatch mechanism beside `packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/`. Now that the design is shipped (§17's cadence included), the model no longer runs ahead of the code, so the duplication buys nothing and can drift silently. Fold it: keep the harness, delete the model, and drive the **real** modules from it.

## The drift surface

| sim.mjs | engine |
|---|---|
| `mostRecentAnchor` / `nextAnchor` / `periodMs` / `LEGACY_FREQUENCIES` | `queue/anchors.mjs`, `calendar.mjs` (its own comment says "mirroring") |
| `statusOf` + the legacy-label decode | `queue/work-item.mjs` |
| `writeBoardRow` / `boardRow` | `queue/schedule-board.mjs` |
| `schedulerRun()` — four jobs, both occurrence guards, adoption, reclaim | `planSchedulerRun` + the shell in `queue/scheduler-run.mjs` |
| `pickable()`, `claim()`, `postClaimVerify()` | `pickOrder`, `claimWinner`, `conflictsWithEarlierClaim` |
| `janitor()` | `queue/janitor-rules.mjs` |
| `eligible` / `gatedModel` / `APPROVAL_RE` | `built-in-tasks.mjs`'s `APPROVAL_RE`, `parseRequestFields` |

## Why it is feasible

- Every GitHub call in `queue/` goes through one function — `gh(path, { method, body })` from `signals/gh.mjs` — over 19 distinct paths (issues, labels, comments, permission, Actions variables, workflow dispatch).
- A fake GitHub at exactly that seam already exists in `test/queue/executor-loop.test.mjs` (~45 lines) and already drives the real `runExecutor` end to end.
- `runExecutor` is already fully injectable: `now`, `random`, `heldNow`, `collectSignalsFor`, `runTaskCodeWork`, `invokeAgent`, `log`.
- The pure cores are already exported: `planSchedulerRun`, `pickOrder`, `claimWinner`, `noGoPlan`, `evaluatePrecondition`, the janitor rules.

The enabling gap: `scheduler-run.mjs`'s shell (`main`, exported as `runSchedulerRun`) is argless — it reads `process.cwd()`, `process.env`, `new Date()`, `makeGh()`. Same for the janitor and drain-dispatch shells. They need `runExecutor`'s parameter shape, with `main()` as the argless wrapper.

## What survives — the harness proper

- the virtual clock and ordered event queue (`seq` modelling comment-id order);
- the platform behaviours: the cron grid / `cronHours`, dropped and late fires, stale snapshots for `raceExecutorsAt`, `eventLost`, the absent/corrupt board, `gone`/`unreadable` issues, the collaborator permission table;
- `actionExecutions()`, which gets stronger: the fake counts the engine's real `workflow_dispatch` calls instead of the model's own runs;
- the scenario DSL — 12 methods across 1994 lines of `scenarios.test.mjs`, whose assertions mostly read the issue store the fake GitHub also has, so most scenarios should port largely intact;
- the README's coverage map and "The unsimulated world" table — the second one becomes literally "what the fake `gh` does not do".

## The cost, accepted deliberately

Two independent expressions of the design can disagree, and the disagreement is a signal; afterwards the scenarios are regression tests against captured behaviour, not a cross-check of implementation against spec. That independence is already given up by the standing rule (*"model what the engine's code actually writes, never the rule's stated intent"*), and the design is shipped, so the oracle role has lapsed. Consequence to land in the same change: the sim README's "change the simulator first" becomes "write the engine's pure core first, drive it from the harness".

## Phasing (one PR per slice)

1. Promote the fake GitHub out of `executor-loop.test.mjs` into a shared world (issue store, comment ids, labels, permission API, Actions variables, dispatch capture), plus the clock and event queue. No behaviour change — the existing loop test proves the fake still works.
2. Give the scheduler-run, janitor and drain shells `runExecutor`'s injectable shape; `main()` becomes the argless wrapper.
3. Port scenarios in slices, deleting the matching sim model as each goes green: anchors, then the board, pick/claim, janitor, requests, the executions accounting last.
4. `sim.mjs` ends as world + DSL only; `coverage.test.mjs` and the README tables carry over.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. - design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: extract-from-conversations
3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch
94	
95	Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:
96	
97	- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
98	- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
99	  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
100	  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
101	  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.
102	
103	The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
104	stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
105	every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
106	breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.
107	
108	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
109	
110	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
111	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
112	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
113	
114	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
115	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
116	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
117	
118	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
119	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
120	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
121	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
122	silence it replaced.
123

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
59	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. This is the first rung to try for any
60	   lesson whose whole logic is "these patterns over these files", and most captured conditions are.
61	2. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
62	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
63	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
64	   to read and maintain for nothing.
65	3. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
66	4. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
67	
68	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
69	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
70	both rungs in [`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
71	
72	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
73	relocates it. When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
74	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
75	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
76	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
77	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
78	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
79	
80	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all.** A trap from misusing a specific API, class, or
81	library goes as a **comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where the next editor of
82	that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list. Co-locate it in a file's own header
83	comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a
84	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
85	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
86	
87	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
88	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
89	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
90	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
91	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
92	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
93	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
94	
95	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
96	
97	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
98	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
99	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
100	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
101

{"number":170,"title":"Revisit: Workflow tool's interactive opt-in blocks unattended routines (waiting on Anthropic)","body":"## The limitation

The multi-agent-orchestration **`Workflow`** tool requires an **interactive human opt-in on every run** ("Allow Claude to run a workflow?"). That prompt only disappears under bypass-permissions / headless modes a scheduler can't be relied on to be in. Because an unattended routine has no human to click **Allow**, any routine that fans out through the Workflow tool stalls on step one.

This also means the tool's nicest ergonomics are off-limits to us for unattended work: committing a Workflow script and having the nightly job just run it by name (`Workflow({name: ...})`) hits the **same** prompt — the gate is on *invoking* a workflow, not on authoring one. And the parallel-agent step can't be pushed into a plain committed script either, since spawning Claude subagents is a harness capability, not something arbitrary code can call.

## Our current workaround

We fan the fleet daily maintenance routine out with **plain subagent dispatch** (the Agent/Task tool) instead, which carries no opt-in gate, and the orchestrator honors the phase barriers itself. See #168 / #169 and `routines/auto-all-repos-maintenance.md` + `skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md`.

This works and is the right default (no dependency on an out-of-repo permission-mode setting), but it costs us the Workflow tool's built-in phase/barrier machinery and the option to run committed, reviewed orchestration code.

## Why keep this open

This is a limitation of the platform, not our code — we're **waiting on the world to change**. If Anthropic later lets an unattended session pre-authorize the Workflow tool (a settings allowlist entry, an environment/routine permission mode that reliably suppresses just this prompt, or persisted per-workflow consent that survives a fresh cloud clone), we could reconsider using committed Workflow scripts for the fleet routine and get determinism + review back.

**Action:** periodically check with Anthropic / the Claude Code release notes whether the Workflow tool can be pre-authorized for unattended sessions. When it can, revisit the plain-dispatch decision in the routine spec.

{"number":1341,"title":"Eliminate the task-janitor: fold its recovery into the scheduler run, its visibility into the dashboard","body":"## The problem

`task-janitor` is the third responsibility of the task machinery (scheduler creates, executor executes, janitor cleans up). Reviewing its four queue rules, none of them earns a daily agentless task of its own: each is either **harmful**, **noise**, or **already someone else's job**.

Owner's verdict, rule by rule:

**A — stale ready** (`ready` for ~2× its period → clear status, park `needs-human:action`)
> So a valid task that just wasn't executed becomes parked?? This seems like it creates more problems than fixes. And the comments are just noise.

The item is *fine*. Nothing is wrong with it except that no executor got to it. Parking it takes a healthy item out of the queue and holds its task's lane, converting a latency symptom into a permanent stop that a human must clear by hand.

**B — dead agent leash** (`agent-running` idle ≥3h → clear status, park `needs-human:decision`)
> The scheduler can identify that and make the status switch.

Structurally identical to the executor-leash reclaim the scheduler run **already** owns as job 3 of `queue/scheduler-run.mjs` — a deterministic, serialized, hourly label rule. There is no judgment in "idle past a clock bound"; it is the same shape, one label name apart, recovering in ~2h instead of ~25h.

**C — stuck dependency** (blocked ≥2 days with blockers open → comment, labels untouched)
> Another noisy comment. The block is there because it's there. No need to make a fuss.

The rule's own comment concedes it: *"Nothing here is stuck mechanically — it will proceed by itself the moment those close."* It changes nothing and posts a comment saying so.

**D — stateless repair** (open item with no state label → park `needs-human:decision`)

## Agreed end state (summary — DESIGN.md §18 is authoritative)

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/` owns the whole task surface: queue, executor, signals, task contract, calendar/anchor math, dispatch, run-records, code-work, delivery helpers (`land-pr`, `deliver-generated`), GitHub REST helpers, the two workflow stubs, the operational `.md`s, and the `implement-request` built-in as an ordinary pack task.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/shared-code/*` is the pack's published import surface — the one sanctioned cross-pack import in the corpus (barriers-enforced). Consumers: claudinite-dashboard (title grammar, outcome decode, anchor math) and every pack task that delivers (delivery + gh helpers).
- Queue meta-machinery relocates in: `task-janitor` (from basics), `usage-fold` (from claudinite-growth), the task-declaration checks (from claudinite-growth worldRules) — and the simulator + scenario suite (`docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/`), the mechanism's executable spec, into the pack's own `test/`.
- The update flows (`updates/*`) move into `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/`; old `updates/*` paths stay as callable shims until no fielded vendored worker names them.
- `converge-wiring` splits: distribution wiring (hooks, rules index, gitattributes, badges) stays engine; workflow/scheduling wiring moves to the pack. Bootstrap stops wiring task machinery; adopting `claudinite-tasks` scaffolds it.
- The `pending-workflows/` withhold lane is deleted: after #1302 and #1290 the member workflow files are static (one-time cron at setup, `run:` lines pointing at stable mount pack paths). A structural YAML change is an explicit human-supported fleet PR event.
- A repo without `claudinite-tasks` runs no scheduled work and updates via a human session (update/adopt-pack skills) — no forced auto-update.
- Wire protocol (item titles, labels, run-record lines) is unchanged; legacy `engine/implement-request` titles decode forever.

## Plan

**Phase 0 — out-of-band setup:** none required. No new secret, permission, or platform setting; #1302 already removed the secrets variance.

**Review pass — one PR stack, approved together:**
- [ ] PR A — create `packs/claudinite-tasks/`: move `engine/scheduler/*` in (with `shared-code/`), leave re-export shims at every old `engine/scheduler/*` path a fielded caller names, adjust the vendor set (operational-`.md` whitelist paths, engine walk), move `engine-tests/scheduler/` **and `docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/` (sim.mjs, scenarios.test.mjs, coverage.test.mjs)** into the pack's `test/` (SCENARIOS.md stays in docs/ as the play-through record, its sim links repointed), add the barriers config sanctioning `shared-code/*`.

- [ ] PR D (gated tail — written and approved now, merged by chain link L4): delete the old-path shims and any withhold leftovers.

**Execution chain** — each link filed as a sub-issue on approval of this plan, `Blocked-by:` the previous:
- [ ] L1 — force `fleet-baseline` with follow; exit: every member's stamp shows the pack version that ships claudinite-tasks, read from stamps, not run conclusions.
- [ ] L2 — manual fleet pass (owner-supported): repoint each member's two workflow files' `run:` lines and the CCR routine stored-prompt pointers (`executor.md`, `queue/instructions.md`) to the mount pack paths; exit: each member's next scheduler run green from the pack path.

- [ ] L4 — merge PR D; exit: fleet self-tests green on the shim-free mount.

{"number":1333,"title":"claudinite-canary-repo: the withhold lane it probes no longer exists","body":"The `claudinite-canary-repo` pack exists to rehearse one thing: the **withhold lane** — a `.github/workflows/` write diverted to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, carried in a maintenance PR, and moved into place by a session holding a credential the Action token does not have.
